title: Achilles Tendinopathy
case: Case: A 38-year-old recreational runner has 3 months of Achilles pain 4 cm above the heel, worst in the morning. The tendon is thickened and tender. Single-leg heel raise reproduces his pain, with fewer repetitions than the other leg. Thompson test is negative. He recently started a new running plan with more hills.

Working diagnosis: midportion Achilles tendinopathy. Plan: education, reduce hills and speed, isometrics for pain, progressive slow heavy calf loading for 12 weeks, plyometrics later, gradual return to hills.

differentials.name: Achilles rupture or tear
differentials.key: Sudden pop, weak push-off, positive Thompson, gap

differentials.name: Paratendinopathy
differentials.key: Swelling and crepitus around the tendon, stays still with movement

differentials.name: Retrocalcaneal bursitis
differentials.key: Pain and swelling in front of the tendon, above the heel
differentials.next: Footwear changes, medical review if persistent

differentials.name: Haglund deformity
differentials.key: Bony prominence at the back of the heel, tight shoes

differentials.name: Plantaris injury or posterior ankle impingement
differentials.key: Deep pain at the back of the ankle

differentials.name: Flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy
differentials.key: Pain deep at the back of the ankle, worse with toe flexion

differentials.name: Spondyloarthritis (enthesitis)
differentials.key: Bilateral heel pain, stiffness, other joints

qa: Why is the Thompson test done? It helps detect a complete rupture, which needs urgent treatment, and which can be mistaken for tendinopathy or a calf strain.
Why are fluoroquinolone antibiotics and steroids asked about? They are associated with tendon damage and rupture.
Why is the insertional type loaded differently? Deep dorsiflexion compresses the tendon against the heel bone and can increase pain.
The patient wants complete rest. What do you say? Complete rest reduces load capacity and often does not cure the problem. Reduce, not remove, the load and build capacity.
Why measure the single-leg heel raise? It is a simple function test that shows reduced capacity and gives a baseline for progress.

fields.Position: Prone with the feet hanging off the bed
fields.Action: Palpate the tendon with a pinch grip from the heel up to the calf. Note thickening, a nodule and the most tender point
fields.Positive: Localised tenderness and thickening that reproduces the familiar pain
fields.Limits: Tenderness is also present in partial tears and paratendinopathy; interpret with other findings

fields.Purpose: Help separate a tendon problem from tissue around the tendon
fields.Action: Find the thickened tender area and ask the patient to move the ankle up and down. Note whether the swelling moves with the tendon and whether pain stays in the same part of the arc
fields.Positive for tendinopathy: The swelling moves with the tendon, and pain appears in a part of the movement arc that changes with ankle position
fields.Positive for tissue around the tendon (p: Swelling stays still and pain is the same through the arc

fields.Action: Palpate the tender area with the ankle in dorsiflexion and then in plantar flexion. In tendinopathy the tenderness lessens or disappears when the tendon is held tight in plantar flexion (the tender area moves with the tendon)
fields.Limits: Limited accuracy; used with the painful arc sign

fields.Position: Prone with the feet hanging off the bed, or kneeling on a chair
fields.Positive: No foot plantar flexion on the affected side
fields.Negative: The foot moves into plantar flexion
fields.Supports: A positive result suggests Achilles rupture and needs urgent referral
fields.Limits: A negative test does not rule out a partial tear. Also check for a palpable gap and weak heel raise

redFlags.Finding: Sudden pop, inability to rise on the toes, positive Thompson test, palpable gap
redFlags.Immediate action: Avoid loading; refer same day or next day

redFlags.Finding: Pain after recent fluoroquinolone antibiotic or steroid use
redFlags.Immediate action: Medical review about medication; avoid heavy loading

redFlags.Finding: Hot red swollen heel with fever
Bilateral heel pain with morning stiffness and other joint or skin signs
Thick painless bilateral nodules with a family history of heart disease

manual.name: Deep friction massage on the tendon

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education and progressive loading. Manual therapy is a minor adjunct. Do not claim to break down scar tissue or realign tendon fibres through manual techniques.

exercise.Steps: Stand with the heels at floor level and rise to
exercise.Starting dose: 5 holds of 30 to 45 seconds, once or twice a day

exercise.Steps: mid-range, hold; or seated with weight on the knee

exercise.Exercise: Seated and standing calf raise (heavy slow resistance)
exercise.Steps: Rise slowly over about 3 seconds, lower over about 3 seconds, adding weight
exercise.Starting dose: 3 sets of 15, then reduce to 12, 10, 8 repetitions as load goes up; 3 days a week for about 12 weeks
exercise.Progress when: Able to complete the sets with good control

exercise.Steps: Stand on a step with the knee straight (and again bent), rise on both feet, lower on the affected leg only
exercise.Starting dose: 3 sets of 15, twice a day, daily for about 12 weeks
exercise.Progress when: Pain settles; add load with a backpack
Pain stays under about 4 out of 10 with no next-day flare

exerciseNotes: Principle: progressive tendon loading is the first-line treatment. Both eccentric heel drops and heavy slow resistance programs have shown benefit, and no program is clearly superior for everyone. Choose the one the patient can do and adhere to. Pain up to about 4 out of 10 during exercise is commonly accepted if it settles within 24 hours and morning stiffness is not worse the next day.

Insertional type modification: avoid dropping the heel below the level of the step (do the heel raise on flat ground or with the heel at step level) and avoid deep dorsiflexion stretches and tight shoes. Heel lifts in shoes may help comfort for a time.
Load management: reduce painful activity rather than stopping completely. Consider replacing some running with cycling or swimming. Keep a log of pain and morning stiffness.
Return to running criteria (example): no more than mild pain, good heel raise capacity compared with the other side, normal walking, and tolerance of hopping. Increase volume and intensity gradually.

modalities.name: Extracorporeal shockwave
modalities.indicated: Option for persistent pain after several months of loading

modalityNotes: Medical options (decided by doctors): corticosteroid injection into or near the tendon is generally avoided because of rupture risk. Other injections and surgery are for persistent cases after a long course of non-surgical care.
pathway: Any emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.
Positive Thompson test or palpable gap? Yes: urgent referral.
Pain and thickening in the tendon 2 to 6 cm above the heel, load-related, with reduced heel raise capacity? Yes: working diagnosis is midportion Achilles tendinopathy.
Pain at the heel attachment with dorsiflexion provocation? Yes: working diagnosis is insertional Achilles tendinopathy.
Start a loading program with load management. Modify the program for insertional type.
If no improvement after a full trial, review the diagnosis and consider specialist options.
Visit 1: screen for rupture and other flags, explain tendinopathy as a load problem, discuss medication risks, set goals.
Early: manage load, begin isometrics for pain relief if needed.
